name: Bulkhead
intent: Split shared resources into isolated compartments, so a failure or slowdown in one part cannot drain the resources the others need.
scenario: One service handles both payments and product search using a single pool of 10 worker threads. The payment provider gets slow, every thread ends up waiting on it, and search stops responding even though search itself is perfectly healthy.
problem: Shared pools (threads, connections, memory, a rate quota) are efficient, but they couple everything that uses them. A single slow dependency or a single noisy tenant can take all of the shared resource, so one problem turns into a total outage.

howItWorks.title: Name the resource that is shared
howItWorks.text: Look for the pool that many kinds of work draw from: a thread pool, a database connection pool, a queue consumer group, memory, or an API quota. If one use can exhaust it, the others are at risk.

howItWorks.title: Give each kind of work its own compartment
howItWorks.text: Create separate pools: for example 5 threads for payments and 5 for search, or a connection pool per downstream service. The name comes from the sealed compartments in a ship's hull: a leak floods one, not the whole vessel.

howItWorks.title: Reject or queue when a compartment is full
howItWorks.text: When the payments pool is full, new payment calls fail fast (or wait in a short bounded queue). They do not borrow threads from search. The damage stays inside the compartment that has the problem.

howItWorks.title: Choose the boundaries that match your risks
howItWorks.text: Isolate by dependency (one pool per downstream), by customer tier (a noisy free tenant cannot starve paying ones), or by priority (health checks and admin tools always have capacity). Separate processes or containers give stronger isolation than separate pools in one process.

howItWorks.title: Size and watch each compartment
howItWorks.text: Splitting reduces flexibility: spare capacity in one pool cannot help another. Size pools from real traffic, and alert on rejections per compartment, because rejections are the signal that something upstream is wrong.

pros: Contains failures: a slow dependency only affects its own compartment
Protects critical functions from less important ones
Pairs well with circuit breakers and timeouts
cons: Lower utilisation: idle capacity in one compartment cannot be used by another
More pools to size, tune and monitor
Too many tiny compartments can cause rejections even when the system as a whole has capacity
Needs thought to choose the right boundaries
whenToUse: A service that calls several downstream dependencies of varying reliability
Multi-tenant systems where one tenant must not starve the rest
Protecting critical paths (checkout, login) from optional features
whenNotToUse: A small system with one dependency, where a split pool only wastes capacity
When you can simply scale out and the failure risk is low
pitfalls: Isolating threads but sharing something else, such as one database connection pool
Compartments sized by guess and never revisited
No timeouts, so even a small compartment fills up and stays full
No alert on rejections, so the contained failure goes unnoticed
